stem.v: A server writes its audit trail to /var/log/billing.log. The team wants nobody, not even root, to overwrite or erase what is already in the file, while the app can keep adding new lines to the end. Which command does this?

options.why: The sticky bit only matters on folders, where it limits who can delete files. Linux ignores it on a regular file.
ACLs only grant read, write and execute. "t" is not an ACL permission, and ACLs cannot make a file append-only.
chattr +a sets the append-only attribute. Existing content cannot be changed or deleted, even by root, but new data can still be added to the end. That is why it suits log files.
setenforce switches SELinux between enforcing (1) and permissive (0). It does not take a file name.

stem.t: A server writes its audit trail to the billing log in the var log folder. Nobody, not even root, may overwrite or erase what is already there, but the app must keep adding new lines. Which command does this?

set F A C L, adding a made-up T permission to the mask.
change attr, setting the append-only attribute on the log file.
set enforce, pointed at the log file.

reason.t: The append-only attribute stops anyone, even root, from changing what is already written, while new lines can still be added.

command.t: The command is: change attr, plus A, slash var, slash log, slash billing dot log.

options.text: Run sudo source /etc/group to reload maria's groups.

options.text: The file can only be written by root, so maria needs sudo.

options.text: maria needs to log out and log back in.

options.text: maria needs extra permissions on the file that she does not have yet.

stem.v: A few help desk staff who connect remotely need to run some admin commands on a Linux server. What is the best way to handle this request?

options.text: Share the root password with them and set PermitRootLogin yes in sshd_config.
options.why: Sharing root's password and allowing direct root SSH logins is a serious security risk, and nobody can tell who did what.

options.text: Ask which commands they need to run with elevated rights and add sudo rules for just those.
options.why: This follows least privilege: each person gets only the commands they need, through sudo, and every use is logged under their own name.

options.text: Set the SUID bit on every program they ask to use.
options.why: SUID would let every user on the system run those programs as their owner, usually root. That is far too broad and very risky.

options.text: Put them in a group that sudoers allows to run any command, so they can switch to root.
options.why: This hands out full root access when they only need a few commands. It breaks least privilege.

total 4

/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/snap/bin
sam@app01:~$ file /usr/local/bin/exportsales
/usr/local/bin/exportsales: POSIX shell script, ASCII text executable
sam@app01:~$ stat -c '%A %U %G' /usr/local/bin/exportsales
-rwxr-xr-x root root
What is the problem and how should it be fixed?

options.text: The script has no execute permission for the user. Add execute permission.
options.why: The mode is rwxr-xr-x, so everyone, including sam, already has execute permission.

options.text: The script is owned by root, so sam cannot run it. Use chown to give it to sam.
options.why: Anyone can run a file that has execute for others, whatever its owner. Ownership is not the problem.

options.text: /usr/local/bin is not in the user's PATH. Add it in the user's .bash_profile.
options.why: The script exists and is executable by everyone, but echo $PATH has no /usr/local/bin, so the shell never looks there and says command not found. Adding that folder to PATH in .bash_profile fixes it for every login.

options.text: The user has the wrong SELinux context for the script. Change the SELinux policy.
options.why: Nothing here shows an SELinux denial. "command not found" means the shell could not find the file at all.

stem.v: An audit finds that several local accounts have kept the same password for over a year. Which command brings an account in line with a rule that passwords must change at least every 90 days?

chage changes password aging, and -M sets the maximum number of days a password may be used. After 90 days the user must pick a new one. (You add the user name at the end, for example chage -M 90 sam.)
loginctl manages login sessions, and -H means run on a remote host. It has nothing to do with password age.
usermod -aG adds a user to groups. 90 is not a group name, and nothing about password age changes.

stem.t: An audit finds several local accounts have kept the same password for over a year. Which command brings an account in line with a rule that passwords must change at least every 90 days?

options.t: password with dash D, which deletes the password.
change age with capital M 90, setting the maximum password age.
login C T L with dash H, which runs on a remote host.
user mod adding the account to a group named 90.

reason.t: Change age with capital M sets the maximum number of days a password may be used before it must change.

command.t: The command is: change age, dash capital M, 90.

stem.t: A new server should be known as web east 07. The change must take effect right away and still be there after a reboot. Which command does this?

stem.v: A contractor's account, pkline, is being disabled, and the contractor still has several programs running on the server. Which command stops every process owned by pkline at once?

options.why: kill expects process IDs, not a user name, so this fails.

This sends a hangup signal to processes named "pkline". It does not target a user's processes and often just reloads programs.

P S with dash U, which only lists the processes.

command.t: The command is: P kill, dash U, P Kline.

stem.v: An admin started a long report with ./build-report.sh & and then ran other commands. Now they want the report back in the foreground of the same terminal so they can watch and interact with it. Which commands do this? (Choose two.)

fg brings a background job to the foreground. %1 picks job number 1 from the jobs list, and plain fg picks the most recent job.

disown removes the job from the shell's job table. Then fg can no longer reach it.

WantedBy= decides which target or unit pulls this service in when it is enabled. It does not set the start order.
